clue.text: Short and extremely sexy movement made by a woman

indicators.note: something taken to extremes goes to its very ends, so only the two end letters of the next word count

blocks.note: a short reply is a curt one
the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: A provocative little move performed by a woman, perhaps on a dance floor.
explanation.definitionFit: A curtsy is the small bob with bent knees that women traditionally make as a gesture of respect.

clue.text: Communist on quiet journey to work

blocks.note: Com. is a standard abbreviation for Communist
making no sound

explanation.surface: A party member travelling silently on the daily trip to the office.
explanation.definitionFit: To commute is to travel regularly between home and one's place of employment.

clue.text: Poirot asked to get hold of duty lists

indicators.note: the phrase has the clue's own words grip a run of letters that lies inside them

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the detective's name and the start of the next word

explanation.surface: Agatha Christie's Belgian detective is asked to obtain the staff schedules.
explanation.walkthrough: Poirot's name looks like a reference to a sleuth, but it only supplies letters: ROTAS spans poiROT ASked.
explanation.definitionFit: Rotas are schedules showing whose turn it is to perform each task or shift.

clue.text: Drink given by school before toddlers' sleeps

indicators.note: in a down entry, coming before means placed first, ahead of the following piece

blocks.note: a standard abbreviation for school
short daytime rests taken by small children

explanation.surface: A nursery hands out something to drink before the little ones have their afternoon rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Schnaps is a strong distilled spirit from Germany and Scandinavia, an alcoholic drink.

clue.text: Balance shown by officer class

blocks.note: Off. is the usual abbreviation for officer
a group or class, as in a school set

explanation.surface: An officer's social rank is said to give a sense of equilibrium.
explanation.definitionFit: An offset is an amount that counterbalances or compensates for another, so it balances things out.

clue.text: Raise and care for chick starting to fly over ridge

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept
in a down entry, being over something means sitting above it, so this piece comes first

blocks.note: the opening letter of the verb
a narrow shelf or ridge of rock

explanation.surface: A young bird learning to fly sets off over a mountain ridge.
explanation.walkthrough: The long definition takes up the start of the clue; the wordplay is only the last four words.
explanation.definitionFit: To fledge a bird is to rear it until its feathers are grown and it can leave the nest.

clue.text: Quiet — sells tins (anag)

indicators.note: the setter openly labels the preceding words as letters to be rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper selling canned goods enjoys a moment of peace and calm.
explanation.walkthrough: A rare clue that names its own device: (anag) tells the solver to rearrange sells tins.
explanation.definitionFit: Stillness is calm and silence, a noun meaning the same as quiet in the sense of peace.

clue.text: Youngster getting Torquay's first American sausage

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

blocks.note: the initial of the Devon seaside town
a weenie is US slang for a frankfurter

explanation.surface: A child on holiday in Torquay, an English seaside town, gets a hot dog.
explanation.definitionFit: A tweenie is a child between infancy and the teenage years, so a youngster of about ten.

clue.text: Mad sunbathers out to get opponents of blood sports

indicators.note: mad means crazed and disordered, so the following letters are thrown into a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Crazed sun-worshippers venture out in order to find people who campaign against fox hunting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out' looks like an anagram signal, but it is part of the fodder; 'Mad' is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Hunt saboteurs are activists who disrupt fox hunts and similar field sports, which they oppose.

clue.text: Give out retro magazine

indicators.note: retro means looking backwards, so the next word is read from its end

blocks.note: Time is the famous American news magazine

explanation.surface: Someone hands out copies of an old-fashioned magazine.
explanation.definitionFit: To emit is to send out or discharge something, such as light, heat or a sound.

clue.text: Women in queenly residences accepting open place to learn to use a needle

indicators.note: something accepting takes others in, so the first piece wraps around what follows

blocks.note: a queen bee lives in a hive
the Open University
stitch with needle and thread

explanation.surface: Ladies in royal palaces take up a spot where they can be taught needlework.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Queenly residences' suggests palaces, but the queen is a bee. The OU, or Open University, is Britain's distance-learning university.
explanation.definitionFit: Housewives are married women who run a household, so they are women in a particular role.

clue.text: Country airs active round America

indicators.note: letters that are active are moving about, so they settle in a new order
to go round something is to surround it, so the rearranged letters enclose the other piece

blocks.note: taken as written
the United States

explanation.surface: A nation broadcasts busy programmes around the United States.
explanation.definitionFit: Russia is the largest nation in the world, spanning eastern Europe and northern Asia.

clue.text: Mark granted a wish to go with the others, uninvited

blocks.note: a label or identifying mark
taken as written
to long for is to wish for

explanation.surface: Someone named Mark gets his wish to join a group that never asked him.
explanation.walkthrough: Mark reads as a man's name, but it is a common noun for a label.
explanation.definitionFit: To tag along is to follow or accompany a group, typically without having been asked.

clue.text: Midweek mash of swede and last of parsley

indicators.note: mashing pulps food into a jumble, so these letters are crushed into a new order
the last of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: taken as written
the final letter of the herb

explanation.surface: The mid-week menu: mashed swede garnished with parsley.
explanation.walkthrough: A swede is a root vegetable, called rutabaga in North America.
explanation.definitionFit: Wednesday is the day falling in the middle of the working week.

clue.text: Arrange to tie one tag in knots

indicators.note: something tied in knots is twisted out of shape, so the letters are tangled into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Instructions for knotting a label onto a parcel.
explanation.definitionFit: To negotiate a deal is to arrange or settle its terms through discussion.

clue.text: Hopeless hiding an iconic footballer

indicators.note: a word that is hiding something conceals it within its own letters

blocks.note: the letters sit in the middle of the word

explanation.surface: A useless player conceals a footballing legend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hopeless' looks like a description of the footballer, but it is the word that contains him.
explanation.definitionFit: Pelé was the Brazilian forward who won three World Cups and is widely regarded as the greatest player ever.

clue.text: Guarded silver in hollow cavity

indicators.note: a hollow thing is emptied of its insides, leaving only the outer letters
one piece placed in another sits inside it

blocks.note: the first and last letters only
Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

explanation.surface: Silver coins are kept safe in a hidden hole.
explanation.definitionFit: Cagy describes someone reluctant to give information, so cautious and guarded in what they say.

clue.text: In taxi, I take home a piece of furniture

blocks.note: another word for a taxi
taken as written
to net a sum is to take it home as pay after deductions

explanation.surface: A passenger carries a bulky item of furniture home in a taxi.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take home' suggests carrying something, but here it means earning, as in take-home pay.
explanation.definitionFit: A cabinet is a cupboard with shelves or drawers for storing or displaying things.

clue.text: Partially conscious, conservative used offensive language

blocks.note: Con. is the abbreviation for a Conservative
to cuss is to swear

explanation.surface: A half-awake Tory politician swore.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone concussed has taken a blow to the head and is dazed, only partly aware.

clue.text: Caught editor tucking into awfully hard cheese

indicators.note: something done awfully is done badly, so the following letters end up out of order
tucking into food puts it inside, so this piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: c is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
the usual abbreviation for editor
taken as written

explanation.surface: A newspaper editor is caught eating a block of very hard cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard cheese' reads as a phrase, but hard is the fodder and cheese the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheddar is a firm English cheese, originally from the Somerset village of the same name.

clue.text: Space given to plants in dishes

indicators.note: one thing given to another is added to it, so the pieces join in sequence

blocks.note: an en is a printer's unit of space
trees are plants

explanation.surface: Room is made for houseplants in pots or bowls.
explanation.definitionFit: Entrées are courses of a meal, main dishes in American usage or the course before the roast in British.

clue.text: Give way about setter as a pet

indicators.note: to be about something is to be around it, so the first piece surrounds the second

blocks.note: to budge is to yield or move
the setter refers to themself as I

explanation.surface: The puzzle setter concedes and agrees to be kept as an animal companion.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often refer to themselves in clues, standing for I or ME.
explanation.definitionFit: A budgie, short for budgerigar, is a small parakeet commonly kept as a cage bird in the home.

clue.text: Obscure university hospital's third contribution to breast reconstruction

indicators.note: the third of a word means its third letter, the only one kept
a reconstruction rebuilds something in a new form, so the letters are put together in a different order

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation
the third letter of the word
taken as written

explanation.surface: A little-known university hospital plays a part in rebuilding breasts after surgery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hospital' wants to give the usual H, but the clue asks for its third letter instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Something abstruse is hard to understand, its meaning obscure to most people.

clue.text: All one's worldly goods consist of a broken tea set

indicators.note: a broken set has its parts scattered, so these letters are put back in another order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone's entire possessions amount to one smashed set of crockery.
explanation.definitionFit: A person's estate is the whole of the property and money they own, especially at death.

clue.text: Turned up perfect piece of bone

indicators.note: in a down entry, turning something upward makes it read from bottom to top

blocks.note: A1 means first-rate, with the 1 written as I
a bit is a piece

explanation.surface: An ideal fragment of skeleton is dug up.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often treat the digit 1 as the letter I, so A1 becomes AI.
explanation.definitionFit: The tibia is the shinbone, the larger of the two bones in the lower leg.

clue.text: At risk of death by exploding grenade

indicators.note: an exploding thing flies apart, so the next word's letters are blown into a new order

blocks.note: death is one's end
taken as written

explanation.surface: A soldier is in danger of being killed by a bomb going off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At risk of death' reads as one phrase, but the definition stops at risk and death starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Something endangered is threatened or in peril, as with species facing extinction.

clue.text: Insect taking time to find a source of sugar

indicators.note: taking something on means adding it, so the second piece joins after the first

blocks.note: a bee is an insect
t is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A bee spends time looking for nectar, its sweet supply.
explanation.walkthrough: The bee and sugar suggest nectar or honey; the sugar source is the root crop.
explanation.definitionFit: Sugar beet is a root crop from which much of the world's table sugar is refined.

clue.text: Sheath of the sword found in tent

indicators.note: a sheath is an outer covering, so only the outside letters of the next word are kept

blocks.note: the first and last letters of the word
the épée is a fencing sword

explanation.surface: A sword's scabbard turns up inside a tent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sheath of the sword' reads as a scabbard, but sheath means just the outer letters of the.
explanation.definitionFit: A teepee is the cone-shaped tent of animal skins used by Plains peoples of North America.

clue.text: Silver coins given for processed grains

blocks.note: first meaning: old English coins worth fourpence
second meaning: hulled grain, especially oats

explanation.surface: Silver money is handed over in payment for milled cereal.
explanation.walkthrough: A groat was an old English silver coin worth four old pennies.
explanation.definitionFit: Groats were medieval silver fourpenny pieces, and groats are also hulled, crushed kernels of oats or other cereals.
